items.title: L13: Delivery pressure while clearance is pending
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls; National Security Vetting guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: A recurring management problem is the gap between a person's start date and the arrival of their clearance. The work is urgent, the new starter is capable, and security vetting is slow. The temptation is to let them in early. The sound approach is to treat the delay as a planning problem, with several options in a sensible order. First, ask whether the person can be productive on work that does not need the clearance, such as induction, learning, background reading at lower classification, or tasks on OFFICIAL material for which their baseline checks are sufficient. Second, ask whether the sensitive work can be reshaped, so that cleared colleagues handle it while the new starter handles related work. Third, ask security whether any interim or conditional arrangement is possible. Where it exists, it is set by security, not the manager, and is normally limited, supervised, risk-assessed and recorded. It is never a way of letting the person quietly see what they have not been cleared to see. Fourth, tell the person honestly what they can and cannot do, so they are not put under pressure to cross lines. Fifth, escalate real delivery risks to your own management rather than solving them by weakening control. Records matter: if interim access was agreed, keep a note of who agreed it, its limits and its end date. Remember also that a lack of clearance is not a comment on the person, and that they should not be disadvantaged in other ways while waiting. Finally, learn from the case: next time, start the vetting process earlier, state the clearance level in the advert if known, and plan start dates around likely timescales rather than hoped-for ones.

questions.prompt: A capable new starter is waiting for clearance and the team is under pressure. What is the sensible first question for the manager?

options.text: Whether the person could simply be given a colleague's login for the sensitive work
Whether the person can do useful work that does not need the pending clearance
Whether the clearance could be treated as granted once the baseline checks are complete
Whether the person would be willing to sign a promise to protect any material they see

questions.hint: Planning around the gap comes before any thought of shortcuts.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a legitimate way to use a new starter while clearance is pending?

options.text: Giving them induction, learning and tasks on OFFICIAL material for which baseline checks suffice
Asking them to read SECRET briefings in the room of a cleared colleague
Letting them attend sensitive meetings provided they take no notes
Giving them read-only access to the sensitive folder on a trial basis

questions.hint: Work within the existing clearance is fine; extra access is not.

questions.prompt: The manager asks whether the sensitive work can be reshaped. What does that mean?

options.text: Reclassifying the sensitive material at a lower level for the duration of the delay
Splitting the sensitive files into small parts so that no single part counts as sensitive
Moving the work to an uncleared contractor, who is not covered by the same delay
Redistributing the sensitive tasks to cleared colleagues so that the new starter handles related, non-sensitive work

questions.hint: Reshaping the work changes who does what, not what the material is.

questions.prompt: Who decides whether an interim or conditional arrangement is possible?

options.text: The line manager, as long as the area's director agrees in writing
The new starter, once they have confirmed that they understand the risks
Security, which sets the limits, rather than the line manager
HR, as part of the process of confirming the start date

questions.hint: Interim arrangements are a security decision.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a properly managed interim arrangement?

options.text: Limited, supervised, risk-assessed and recorded, with an end date
Informal, flexible and dependent on the manager's judgement of the person
Open-ended, to be ended when the clearance arrives
Unrecorded, so that the person is not stigmatised by it

questions.hint: Controls and records distinguish an arrangement from a shortcut.

questions.prompt: Why should the manager tell the new starter plainly what they can and cannot do?

options.text: So that any breach can be blamed on the person rather than on the manager who allowed it
So that any breach can be blamed on the person rather than the manager
So they are not put under pressure to cross lines or to guess what is allowed
So they can apply for the clearance themselves if it is delayed further

questions.hint: Clarity protects the person and the information.

questions.prompt: A delivery deadline is at risk because of the delay. What is the right response?

options.text: Quietly give the person access, and report it afterwards once the deadline has been met safely
Ask the cleared colleagues to share their credentials to speed the work
Ask the person to resign and reapply once the clearance has been issued
Escalate the delivery risk to management rather than weaken the security control

questions.hint: Delivery risks are escalated, not solved by relaxing security.

questions.prompt: Interim access was agreed with security. What should the manager keep?

options.text: Nothing in writing, to avoid leaving a trail that could embarrass the person
A record of who agreed it, what its limits are and when it ends
A private note of how the person performed under the interim arrangement
A copy of the person's personal vetting form for reference

questions.hint: Records show control and accountability.

questions.prompt: What does waiting for clearance say about the new starter?

options.text: That the vetting authority has already identified some initial concerns about them as an individual
That their baseline checks were incomplete
Nothing negative, and they should not be disadvantaged in other respects
That they should be placed on a longer probation period, to reflect the time they have waited

questions.hint: Delay is administrative and says nothing about the person.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible lesson for next time?

options.text: Recruit only people who already hold the highest level of clearance
Avoid advertising the clearance level so that candidates are not put off
Promise start dates in the offer letter to encourage candidates to accept
Start vetting earlier and plan start dates around realistic rather than hoped-for timescales

questions.hint: Planning around realistic timescales reduces the pressure.

items.title: L13: Handling a cleared colleague's difficulties
items.source: National Security Vetting guidance; Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: A cleared colleague's difficulties raise two duties that can seem to pull in opposite directions: care for the person and protection of information. Good managers do both, and know where the limits are. Suppose a cleared team member discloses a gambling problem and mounting debts, or a relationship under strain that is affecting their work, or heavy drinking, or contact with someone abroad who has started to ask about their job. Each can increase vulnerability, whether to pressure from others or to poor judgement. The principle is to respond early and proportionately. Listen without judgement. Explain that the department has a reporting route for changes in circumstances and that early reporting is usually seen as responsible. Signpost to support such as an employee assistance service, occupational health and welfare staff. Do not promise confidentiality you cannot give: you may have to pass information to security, although you should share only what is needed. Do not carry out your own investigation, search the person's belongings, or contact their family. Do not decide that the person's clearance should be removed; that is a matter for the vetting authority and the security team, who will look at the whole picture, including any support in place. If you see signs of concern that the person has not reported, such as unexplained wealth, secretive contacts or a sudden interest in material outside their role, raise it with security without delay and without confronting the individual. Keep your notes factual. Treat the person with respect throughout, because people who feel supported are more likely to be open, and because most such situations are resolved without harm.

questions.prompt: A cleared team member discloses a gambling problem and mounting debts. What is the best first response?

options.text: Tell them that they must step down from the team until the debts have been cleared in full
Listen without judgement, explain the reporting route and signpost to support
Ask them to hand over bank statements so that you can judge the scale
Contact their family to arrange help and to check how serious the problem is

questions.hint: Early, supportive response comes before any other step.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager not promise absolute confidentiality to a colleague who discloses a difficulty?

options.text: Information may have to be passed to security, although only what is needed
Managers are forbidden to keep any information about team members private
Information given in confidence is automatically recorded on the personnel file
The colleague's family has a right to be informed of any disclosure

questions.hint: Be honest about the limits of confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Which action goes beyond a manager's proper role?

options.text: Pointing the person to an employee assistance service
Carrying out their own investigation, including searching the person's belongings
Explaining that early reporting is usually seen as responsible
Making a factual note of what the person said

questions.hint: Managers support and signpost; they do not investigate.

questions.prompt: Who decides whether a person's clearance should be affected by a change of circumstances?

options.text: The line manager, who knows the person best
The person's colleagues, who see them every day
The vetting authority and security team, looking at the whole picture
The HR team, using the attendance record

questions.hint: That judgement belongs to security and vetting specialists.

questions.prompt: A cleared colleague has started to receive friendly messages from someone abroad who asks about their job. What should the manager advise?

options.text: Reply politely to the contact and avoid sharing anything sensitive
Block the contact, but say nothing to the department
Wait to see whether the contact asks for something improper
Report the contact to security promptly

questions.hint: Contact asking about work is reportable.

questions.prompt: A manager sees signs such as unexplained wealth and secretive contacts, but the colleague has reported nothing. What is the right course?

options.text: Raise it with security without delay and without confronting the person
Confront the colleague privately and ask for an explanation first
Confront the colleague privately and ask for an explanation before telling anyone else about it
Share the concern with the team to see whether others have noticed

questions.hint: Report without investigating or confronting.

questions.prompt: Why does respectful treatment of the person matter for security?

options.text: People who feel supported are more likely to be open and to report early
Respect is a legal condition for retaining a clearance
Respect is a legal condition for retaining a clearance, and managers may lose theirs without it
Respect reduces the paperwork needed for the review

questions.hint: Support encourages openness.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good note to make after a conversation about a difficulty?

options.text: A note of the manager's view on the person's character
A list of rumours the manager has heard from others
A short, factual note of what was said and what was agreed
A note comparing the person with colleagues who had similar problems

questions.hint: Notes should be factual.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of treating every disclosure as a reason to remove access immediately?

options.text: The vetting authority will refuse to accept any later disclosures
The person will be entitled to automatic promotion
The department will be obliged to pay compensation in every case
Staff stop disclosing, so the department loses early awareness and the chance to support them

questions.hint: Disproportionate reactions discourage honesty.

questions.prompt: Why is a quick, proportionate response usually best for a vulnerable colleague?

options.text: Delays of any kind are punished by the Civil Service Commission, which reviews every response
Problems tend to grow if they are ignored, and support is easier early
Early responses are required by the Official Secrets Act
Quick responses always result in the clearance being withdrawn

questions.hint: Early support reduces harm.

items.title: L13: Competing priorities in a security incident
items.source: Government Functional Standard for Security; departmental incident guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Real incidents rarely present one clean choice. Several good objectives can compete: containing harm, preserving evidence, notifying the right people, and keeping operations running. A manager needs a way of thinking about trade-offs. A helpful rule is that containment and reporting come first, because both are time-critical, while investigation and blame can wait. Take a phishing click on a shared team laptop. Disconnecting the device from the network, or asking security to do so, limits the spread. That may disturb evidence, so the manager should tell security what has happened before powering anything off. Take a misdirected email containing personal data. Recalling it is worth trying, but a recall may not work and must not delay the internal report. Take a lost phone containing work email. Remote lock or wipe is the priority, which means telling the right team quickly. Take a suspected insider who may be copying files. Here the manager should not confront the person or tamper with the account. Alert security or the nominated route and let specialists decide how to preserve evidence and protect people. Keep communications limited: those who need to know should know, and nobody should speculate in group messages. Write down a timeline as you go, including when you learned of the incident and when you reported it, because later reviews and any regulator will ask. When the dust settles, assess whether the incident was a one-off or a symptom, and agree improvements. Good practice is to treat the person who made a mistake fairly, because a culture of fear hides the next incident.

questions.prompt: Which two objectives usually come first when an incident is discovered?

options.text: Establishing who is to blame and informing the whole department
Containing the harm and reporting to the right people
Preserving every item of evidence and resuming normal work
Writing a full report and agreeing improvements

questions.hint: Containment and reporting are time-critical.

questions.prompt: A shared team laptop has been infected after a phishing click. What should the manager do before anything is powered off?

options.text: Switch the device off at once and wipe it to remove the infection
Keep using the laptop until the end of the day, so that work is not lost
Tell security what has happened, so they can decide how to contain it and preserve evidence
Ask a colleague who is good with computers to investigate

questions.hint: Containment can disturb evidence, so security decides.

questions.prompt: A recall of a misdirected email has been attempted. What follows?

options.text: The matter is closed if the recall appears to have succeeded and the recipient has not replied
The report can wait until the recall has been confirmed
The report is needed only if the recipient replies
The internal report is still made at once, whether or not the recall worked

questions.hint: A recall may fail and must not delay reporting.

questions.prompt: A phone containing work email is lost on a train. What is the priority?

options.text: Telling the right team quickly so that it can be locked or wiped remotely
Searching the train for the phone before telling anyone
Waiting until the end of the day to see whether the phone is handed in
Changing the owner's personal passwords, but leaving the work accounts for later in the week

questions.hint: Speed matters for remote lock or wipe.

questions.prompt: A manager suspects a colleague of copying files they should not. What is the right course?

options.text: Confront the colleague and ask them to explain what they are doing
Alert security or the nominated route and let specialists decide how to proceed
Disable the colleague's account to stop the copying
Gather evidence by reading the colleague's emails and files without telling security first

questions.hint: Do not confront or tamper; report.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager avoid speculation in group messages about an incident?

options.text: Group messages are not retained and so cannot be used as evidence
Speculation is a breach of the Equality Act
Communications should be limited to those who need to know, and speculation can spread harm or unfairness
Only the press office is allowed to use group messages

questions.hint: Limit communications.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager write a timeline as an incident unfolds?

options.text: A timeline is required before the incident can be reported to security or any other body
A timeline replaces the need for an incident report
A timeline is needed only for incidents involving contractors
Later reviews and any regulator will ask when it was learned and reported

questions.hint: Timelines support accountability.

questions.prompt: After an incident, what question should be asked beyond fixing it?

options.text: Whether it was a one-off or a symptom of a wider weakness
Whether the person responsible should be moved out of the team
Whether the incident was serious enough to be recorded
Whether the team's budget can bear the cost

questions.hint: Look for patterns and improvements.

questions.prompt: Why is fair treatment of the person who made a mistake important for security?

options.text: Fair treatment is required before any report can be made
Fair treatment lets the person keep their clearance in every case
A culture of fear hides the next incident
Fair treatment removes the need for any investigation

questions.hint: Fear suppresses reporting.

questions.prompt: When might it be reasonable to delay a report to gather more facts?

options.text: Whenever the manager thinks the incident is minor
When the incident occurs on a Friday afternoon
When the person responsible asks for a little more time to put things right before it is reported
Almost never, because reports can be updated as more facts emerge

questions.hint: Report first, refine later.

items.title: L13: Assessing a data breach: risk and next steps
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; UK GDPR, GOV.UK
items.body: Departmental specialists decide whether a personal data breach must be reported to the ICO and whether individuals must be told, but a manager who understands how the assessment works will give better facts and take better first steps. The core question is whether the breach is likely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms, and whether that risk is high. Several factors are weighed. The type of data matters: contact details are less sensitive than financial data, health data, data about children or vulnerable people, or information revealing sexual orientation, religion or criminal records. The volume matters, though a small breach involving highly sensitive data can be more serious than a large one involving trivial data. The ease of identification matters: names with addresses are easier to link to a person than anonymised figures. The recipient matters: an unintended recipient who is trustworthy and has confirmed deletion is lower risk than the open internet. Security measures matter: encryption that was properly applied may mean the data was not intelligible to those who gained access. Potential consequences matter: identity fraud, discrimination, physical harm, distress or loss of confidentiality. Where the breach is likely to result in a risk, the ICO must be notified without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours of becoming aware. Where it is likely to result in a high risk, those affected must be told without undue delay, in clear language that explains what has happened, the likely consequences and what the organisation is doing, and gives a contact point. All breaches are recorded, including the reasoning for not reporting. A processor, such as a contractor handling data for the department, must tell the department without undue delay if it finds a breach.

questions.prompt: A small breach exposes the health records of a handful of vulnerable people. A larger breach exposes work phone numbers of hundreds of staff. How do these compare?

options.text: The larger breach is always more serious, because volume is decisive
The small breach may be more serious because of the sensitivity of the data
They are equally serious, as both are breaches
Neither needs any special consideration, as the numbers involved in each case are small

questions.hint: Sensitivity can outweigh volume.

questions.prompt: Which factor might mean exposed data was not intelligible to those who gained access?

options.text: Encryption that was properly applied
The use of a long file name
The time of day when the breach happened
The grade of the staff member involved

questions.hint: Proper encryption can reduce risk.

questions.prompt: Why is it easier to assess the risk where a recipient has confirmed deletion?

options.text: Confirmed deletion means that the breach did not occur
A trustworthy recipient who has deleted the data lowers the likelihood of harm
Deletion removes the need to record the breach
Confirmed deletion is required by the ICO before any assessment of the risk can take place

questions.hint: The recipient and containment affect risk.

questions.prompt: Which potential consequence is relevant when weighing risk?

options.text: Embarrassment for the department's press office, which would need to prepare a public statement
The inconvenience of changing a distribution list
Identity fraud, discrimination, distress or physical harm
The cost of sending a reminder email

questions.hint: Impact on individuals is the focus.

questions.prompt: What must a notification to affected individuals generally contain?

options.text: What has happened, the likely consequences, what is being done and a contact point, in clear language
A legal justification for the department's actions
A statement that the department accepts no responsibility
The names of the staff involved in the breach

questions.hint: Clear, useful information is the goal.

questions.prompt: A contractor handling personal data for the department discovers a breach. What should it do?

options.text: Wait to see whether the department notices
Report it only to its own insurers
Fix it and report it in its next annual statement
Tell the department without undue delay

questions.hint: A processor must inform the controller promptly.

questions.prompt: The specialists decide a breach does not need to be reported to the ICO. What should the department still do?

options.text: Delete the records, since no report to the ICO was needed and nothing else follows from it
Record the breach and the reasoning for not reporting it
Report it to the ICO anyway, for completeness, since the department cannot be criticised for doing so
Send a notice to everyone in the department

questions.hint: All breaches are recorded.

questions.prompt: Why is names with addresses a higher risk than anonymised figures?

options.text: They are always classified as special category data, which is subject to stricter rules
They must be encrypted by law
They can be published without restriction
They make it easy to identify and contact individuals

questions.hint: Ease of identification affects risk.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the roles correctly?

options.text: Managers decide on notification, using their judgement of the risk
Affected individuals decide whether the ICO is told
Specialists decide on notification, using the facts the manager and others provide
The press office decides on notification, after it has dealt with any queries from the public

questions.hint: Roles should be respected.

questions.prompt: What does 'high risk' trigger that 'risk' alone does not?

options.text: A duty to tell the affected individuals directly
A requirement to dismiss the staff member involved
A requirement for criminal prosecution
An obligation to close the system concerned

questions.hint: High risk triggers individual notification.

items.title: L13: Layered conflicts of interest
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Recruitment Principles, GOV.UK
items.body: Conflicts of interest become hard when they overlap or when the facts are ambiguous. A manager needs to think in layers. The first layer is the interest itself: financial, family, personal, professional or reputational. The second is the decision it could touch: a recruitment, a contract, a grant, a regulatory decision, a policy choice or a performance rating. The third is the proximity of the person to that decision: do they decide, advise, score, supply information, or merely sit in the same office? The closer the person is to the decision, the greater the need to step back. The fourth is the timing: has the decision been made, is it live, or is it in the future? The fifth is how the situation would look to an informed outsider. Consider examples. A manager who owns shares in a company that is a minor subcontractor to a bidder has an indirect interest, which should still be declared so that others can judge. A senior official whose spouse works for a body that is regulated by the department may need to avoid regulatory decisions affecting that body. A manager whose former employer is bidding must consider how recent the employment was, whether a pension or payment remains, and whether personal loyalties could be thought to exist. A manager who line manages a relative should declare it and arrange for someone else to manage the person, particularly in appraisal, pay and promotion. A declared conflict should result in a recorded decision: who judged it, what they decided, and what actions were agreed, including a review date. Mere declaration does not solve a conflict; it gives others the chance to. The worst outcomes arise from silent assumptions, such as a belief that a small interest cannot matter.

questions.prompt: A manager owns shares in a company that is a minor subcontractor to a bidder. What is the right approach?

options.text: Declare it, even though it is an indirect interest, so others can judge
Ignore it, as the interest is too remote to matter
Sell the shares quietly before the bids are opened and say nothing about the history of ownership
Wait to see whether the bidder wins before deciding

questions.hint: Indirect interests may still need declaring.

questions.prompt: Which factor in assessing a conflict concerns how close the person is to the decision?

options.text: Whether the person is of the same grade as the decision-maker
Whether they decide, advise, score or supply information, rather than merely sitting in the same office
Whether the person has worked in the department for longer than the decision-maker
Whether the person attended the meeting at which the decision was discussed

questions.hint: Proximity increases the need to step back.

questions.prompt: A manager whose spouse works for a body regulated by the department is about to be involved in a regulatory decision about that body. What is the best step?

options.text: Make the decision but ask a colleague to check it
Make the decision, since the spouse is employed by the body and is not the regulated body itself
Say nothing unless the spouse is promoted
Declare the link and avoid being involved in decisions affecting that body

questions.hint: Close family links to regulated bodies require stepping back.

questions.prompt: A bidder is the former employer of an evaluator. What should the evaluator consider declaring?

options.text: Only whether the employer is a large company
Only whether the evaluator liked working there
How recent the employment was, whether any pension or payments remain, and whether loyalties might be thought to exist
Nothing, since the employment ended

questions.hint: Recent or continuing links need consideration.

questions.prompt: A manager line-manages a close relative. What is the right approach?

options.text: Manage the relative as normal, but record that the process was fair
Ask the relative to apply for a transfer to another team
Keep the relationship private, since the relative's work is good
Declare it and arrange for someone else to manage the person, especially for appraisal, pay and promotion

questions.hint: Reporting lines with relatives need changing.

questions.prompt: Why does timing matter when assessing a conflict?

options.text: Conflicts expire after a fixed number of months, so only recent ones need to be considered
Only decisions made at the end of the financial year are covered
A live decision carries more risk than one already made or one far in the future
Past conflicts are always more serious than present ones

questions.hint: Whether a decision is live affects the risk.

questions.prompt: What should a recorded decision on a conflict include?

options.text: Only the name of the person who declared it
Who judged it, what they decided, what actions were agreed and a review date
Only the date of the declaration
A statement that the person has no further obligations

questions.hint: Records should show a managed process.

questions.prompt: Why is mere declaration not enough?

options.text: It gives others the chance to manage the conflict, but it does not resolve it by itself
Declaration is only valid if made in writing to the Commission
Declaration removes the interest but not the potential for bias
Declaration is required only for conflicts that have already caused harm

questions.hint: Declaring is the first step.

questions.prompt: Which assumption is most dangerous?

options.text: That a manager should ask for advice and a second opinion whenever they are unsure of their position
That a conflict can change over time
That a small interest cannot matter, so no declaration is needed
That an outsider might see the situation differently

questions.hint: Silent assumptions are the worst outcomes.

questions.prompt: What question reflects the 'informed outsider' test?

options.text: How would it look to the person's closest friend, who knows them better than anyone else?
How would the situation look to someone who knew all the facts?
How would it look to the press office?
How would it look if the facts were kept private?

questions.hint: The outsider's view is the test.

items.title: L13: Gifts, hospitality and reciprocity
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code, GOV.UK
items.body: Gifts and hospitality are closely tied to a wider principle of reciprocity: when someone does a favour, people feel an urge to return it. That is why a small gift can have a large effect and why public bodies are careful. A manager's role is to see the pattern, not just the single item. A register helps because it can reveal repeated offers from one supplier, clusters of invitations before a decision, or one person who receives much more than others. A single lunch may be harmless, whereas a series of lunches, tickets and invitations during a contract renewal is not. The decision should consider who is offering, what decision may be pending, the size and frequency of the offer, the purpose, and whether the offer is made to the department or to the person. It should also consider whether declining would cause damage which could be mitigated by hosting a meeting on official premises, paying your own way, or sending a polite reply. Where you are the host, the same rules apply in reverse: you should not offer hospitality that would be hard to justify, particularly to people who make decisions affecting your department. For events involving ministers or senior leaders, the department often has a separate process. Some offers should be reported even if declined, because they may be part of a pattern, for example if a supplier makes repeated attempts to give you something after a refusal. A record of declined offers is a useful early warning for the department. If you realise you have accepted something that you should not have, tell your manager promptly, offer to return it or pay for it, and record it. Honest correction is better than concealment.

questions.prompt: Why can even a small gift have a disproportionate effect on judgement?

options.text: Small gifts are taxed as income, which gives the giver a legal claim on the person who receives them
Gifts raise the classification of any information the recipient later handles
Any gift at all counts as an offence under the Official Secrets Act
People feel pressure to return favours, so a small kindness can create a sense of obligation

questions.hint: Reciprocity is the underlying risk.

questions.prompt: What can a register of gifts and hospitality help a manager to see that a single entry cannot?

options.text: Patterns, such as repeated offers from one supplier or a cluster just before a decision
Which colleagues are the most popular with suppliers and stakeholders
The market value of every item offered to the department over the last decade, listed by supplier
Which suppliers deserve to be added to the department's approved list

questions.hint: Registers reveal patterns across time and people.

questions.prompt: Which scenario is the most worrying for a manager reviewing the register?

options.text: A single working lunch at a meeting called to discuss the contract itself
A branded pen handed out to every attendee at a supplier conference
A run of lunches, tickets and invitations from one supplier during a contract renewal
A thank-you card sent by a service user after a successful case, with a small box of chocolates

questions.hint: Pattern, timing and live decisions matter more than any single item.

questions.prompt: How might a manager decline an offer without damaging a good working relationship?

options.text: Accept the offer but make clear to the supplier that you do not expect to enjoy it much
Offer to hold the meeting on official premises, or to pay your own way
Say that the supplier is not significant enough to merit the offer
Delay replying until the date of the event has passed

questions.hint: Practical alternatives preserve the relationship.

questions.prompt: A manager is hosting a supplier meeting and wants to offer a generous lunch. What principle applies?

options.text: Hosting is not covered by the rules, since the manager is not accepting anything from the supplier
Lavish hospitality is acceptable if the manager pays from personal funds
Hospitality is acceptable if the supplier will provide some in return
The same rules apply in reverse, so hospitality offered must not be hard to justify

questions.hint: Giving is covered as well as receiving.

questions.prompt: A supplier keeps trying to give you something after you refused the first time. What should you do?

options.text: Report the pattern to your manager, even though you declined each time
Say nothing further, since you have refused and the matter is closed
Accept a later offer, to avoid causing offence by continuing to refuse
Suggest that the supplier send the item to a colleague instead

questions.hint: Declined offers can still form a worrying pattern.

questions.prompt: Why is a record of declined offers useful to a department?

options.text: It is needed to work out the benefits that are taxable for staff
It is a required part of every security clearance review
It is an early warning of attempts to build influence
It shows suppliers how generous the department has been

questions.hint: Declined offers are still information about risk.

questions.prompt: You realise you accepted hospitality that you should have declined. What is the best course?

options.text: Tell your manager promptly, offer to repay or return it, and record it
Keep quiet, because the value was small and the event has already taken place
Give the item to a colleague so that you no longer hold it
Wait to see whether anybody raises the matter before saying anything

questions.hint: Honest correction is better than concealment.

questions.prompt: Which question helps a manager judge an offer made to a whole team?

options.text: Would the team enjoy the event and be grateful for the offer?
Who is offering, what decision is pending, and what are the size and purpose of the offer?
Has the team been to a similar event in the past year?
Is the offering organisation a large and well-known company?

questions.hint: Context decides.

questions.prompt: For events involving ministers or senior leaders, what do departments often have?

options.text: Nothing beyond the usual rules, since ministers make their own decisions
A requirement that officials attend only in a private capacity and at their own personal expense
An exemption for any hospitality offered at official events
A separate process alongside the usual gifts and hospitality rules

questions.hint: Special processes often apply.

items.title: L13: Borderline outside interests and political connections
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: Real cases rarely fit the categories neatly. A manager is often asked for advice on borderline situations, or has to judge their own. The principles are to act impartially, avoid conflicts, protect the reputation of the Civil Service and follow the department's rules, which differ in detail. Consider a few examples. A civil servant's partner is a candidate in a local election. The civil servant is not standing, but may be seen helping the campaign. They should check the rules, avoid using official resources, and think about how visible their involvement could be, especially if their role is linked to the area. A manager wants to write a paid article or give a paid talk on a topic related to their work. This normally needs permission, and care is needed over what official knowledge is used. A civil servant volunteers for a campaign group which lobbies on an issue connected to their policy area. That may be a conflict, depending on the role, and the department may restrict involvement or ask the person to step back from related work. A civil servant who owns rental property or runs a small business may have no conflict, but if the business supplies the department or its contractors, it does. Another example is an elected role, such as a parish councillor. Rules differ by category of post, and permission is often required. The sound approach is to declare early, give a full picture, ask for a decision in writing, and follow any conditions. Do not argue that an activity is private if others might reasonably see it as connected with your job, and review it as circumstances change.

questions.prompt: A civil servant's partner is standing in a local election. What should the civil servant do?

options.text: Resign at once, since a partner's candidacy is incompatible with civil service work
Take no precautions, because the civil servant is not standing themselves
Endorse the partner publicly, using their official job title for credibility
Check the rules, avoid using official resources and consider how visible their own involvement may be

questions.hint: Involvement may need care even where you are not standing.

questions.prompt: A manager is offered payment to write an article on a topic related to their work. What is the usual position?

options.text: It is allowed so long as the fee is declared for tax purposes
It normally needs permission, with care over any official knowledge used
It is banned in every circumstance, whatever the topic or the publication
It needs no permission if written entirely outside working hours

questions.hint: Paid outside work linked to duties normally needs approval.

questions.prompt: A civil servant volunteers for a campaign group lobbying on an issue in their own policy area. How might this be treated?

options.text: It is a private matter that need not be mentioned to anyone
It is a criminal offence in every case under the Code
It may be a conflict, so the department may restrict involvement or ask them to step back from related work
It is fine so long as they never use their job title

questions.hint: Connected campaigning can conflict with duties.

questions.prompt: A civil servant runs a small business that supplies one of the department's contractors. What is the position?

options.text: It is a link that should be declared and managed, since it touches the department's supply chain
It is not a conflict, because the department itself is not the customer
It is not a conflict as long as the business is small
It becomes a conflict only if the business grows large enough to employ others

questions.hint: Supply-chain links can create conflicts.

questions.prompt: A civil servant wants to become a parish councillor. What is the right approach?

options.text: Stand, and tell the department afterwards if elected
Stand but avoid using their job title in the campaign
Assume that local roles are always allowed for everyone
Check the category of their post and ask for permission before standing

questions.hint: Rules differ by post category and permission is often needed.

questions.prompt: What should a request about an outside interest contain?

options.text: A partial description, so that the department does not over-react
A verbal comment made informally to a colleague who works nearby
A full picture of the interest, a request for a decision in writing and acceptance of any conditions
A statement that the interest is private and so needs no reply

questions.hint: Full disclosure supports a proper decision.

questions.prompt: Why is arguing that an activity is 'private' a risky position?

options.text: Others may reasonably see it as connected with your job
Private activities are always forbidden for civil servants
Private activities are covered by the Official Secrets Act
Private activities cannot be declared under the rules

questions.hint: Perception matters as well as intention.

questions.prompt: A civil servant holds a charity role that had no link with their work, but the charity now bids for funding from their department. What should they do?

options.text: Do nothing, since the role was approved when it started
Tell the department that the position has changed so that it can be reassessed
Resign from the charity at once without explaining why
Wait to see whether the bid succeeds before saying anything

questions.hint: Circumstances change, so declarations need review.

questions.prompt: Which attitude is best for a borderline case?

options.text: Decide privately that the activity is acceptable and carry on
Wait for someone to complain before raising it
Ask a friend in another department what they would do
Declare early and let the department decide, rather than relying on private judgement

questions.hint: Early disclosure is safest.

questions.prompt: Why should outside interests be reviewed at intervals?

options.text: Roles and circumstances change, and an interest with no link can later acquire one
The forms used to record them expire after a fixed time
The Civil Service Commission requires every interest to be reviewed each year
A person's grade may change and with it the rules on interests

questions.hint: Reviews keep declarations current.

items.title: L13: Secrets, transparency and pressure points
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; National Security Act 2023; Freedom of Information Act 2000, legislation.gov.uk
items.body: Civil servants work in a system that values both secrecy for some matters and openness for others. The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives the public a right to request information held by public authorities, subject to exemptions, including for national security, international relations and the formulation of policy. That does not make unauthorised disclosure acceptable. Information is released through the proper process, with decisions made by people responsible for them, not by individuals who feel it ought to be public. The Official Secrets Act 1989 applies to disclosure outside the process. Several pressure points challenge managers. A journalist may contact a team member directly, perhaps apparently well informed. The right reaction is to say nothing about the work, refer them to the press office, and tell the manager. A parliamentary committee may ask a civil servant for evidence. Civil servants generally give evidence on behalf of their ministers and follow guidance on how to do so, and sensitive matters may need clearance. A contractor working for the department is bound by confidentiality and may be notified as being subject to the Official Secrets Act, so managers should make sure that contractors understand what they may and may not share. Family and friends may ask about your work. You can say what you do in general terms but not details, and you should remember that casual chat can add up. When someone leaves, remind them of their continuing duties. Where information is mistakenly published, report at once so it can be taken down and any harm limited. If someone believes information is being withheld improperly, the route is internal challenge or the procedures in the Code, not a leak. Leaks damage trust with ministers, partners and the public, and make officials less willing to put things in writing.

questions.prompt: What does the Freedom of Information Act 2000 give the public?

options.text: A right to see any document held by any department with no exceptions
A right to question any civil servant in person about their work
A right to request information held by public authorities, subject to exemptions
A right to be told about every security incident

questions.hint: FOI is a right with exemptions.

questions.prompt: A journalist contacts a team member directly with apparently well-informed questions. What should the team member do?

options.text: Answer the questions that seem harmless, to keep the relationship friendly
Say nothing about the work, refer the journalist to the press office and tell the manager
Confirm or correct what the journalist says, to make sure it is accurate
Ignore the contact and tell nobody, since the team member did not say anything of substance

questions.hint: Use the proper route.

questions.prompt: Why must unauthorised disclosure not be justified by a belief that information ought to be public?

options.text: Release should happen through the proper process, with decisions taken by those responsible
Individuals are always better placed than the department to decide what is public
The press has a right to any information it asks for once a request has been refused
Disclosure is lawful whenever the person believes it is in the public interest

questions.hint: The proper process decides.

questions.prompt: On whose behalf do civil servants generally give evidence to parliamentary committees?

options.text: Themselves, as individuals, without any need for guidance
The opposition parties, where they request it
Their ministers, following guidance on how to do so
The Civil Service Commission, which prepares them

questions.hint: Civil servants appear on behalf of ministers.

questions.prompt: A contractor works for the department. What should a manager make sure of?

options.text: That the contractor is treated as a member of the public in all respects
That the contractor is exempt from confidentiality duties
That the contractor may discuss anything once the contract ends
That the contractor understands what they may and may not share

questions.hint: Contractors need clear boundaries.

questions.prompt: A friend asks detailed questions about your work at a social gathering. What is the sensible response?

options.text: Share what you can, provided nothing is marked secret
Describe your work in general terms without detail, remembering that casual chat can add up
Share everything, since it is a private setting among friends
Refuse even to say which department you work for

questions.hint: General terms only.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager remind someone who is leaving of their continuing duties?

options.text: Obligations of confidentiality continue after employment ends
Leavers become subject to new rules on departure
Continuing duties apply only if the leaver joins a competitor
Leavers have no duties after their notice period

questions.hint: The duty continues.

questions.prompt: Information is mistakenly published on the department's website. What should happen?

options.text: It should be left until someone complains
It should be taken down quietly by whoever noticed it first, without telling anyone else
It should be reported at once so it can be taken down and any harm limited
It should be reported at the next team meeting

questions.hint: Report promptly.

questions.prompt: Someone believes information is being improperly withheld. What is the proper route?

options.text: Passing it to a journalist
Internal challenge or the Code's procedures, not a leak
Posting it on social media
Giving it to a campaigner

questions.hint: Leaks are not the route.

questions.prompt: What is one effect of leaks on the way government works?

options.text: They increase the amount of information that is published
They help ministers to take better decisions
They reduce the number of security incidents
They damage trust and make officials less willing to put things in writing

questions.hint: Leaks harm trust.

items.title: L13: When the Code route fails
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; Civil Service Commission, GOV.UK
items.body: Sometimes a concern is raised properly and nothing happens. Perhaps the manager responds defensively, the concern is closed without explanation, or the person raising it suffers consequences. At that point there are further steps, and a manager who understands them is better able to support a colleague and to avoid causing the problem. The Civil Service Code says that if you have raised a matter and do not believe it has been dealt with properly, you can take it to the Civil Service Commission. The Commission can receive concerns that the Code has been breached, and complaints from civil servants who believe they have been asked to act in a way that conflicts with it. It is independent of the department and can investigate. Under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, workers who make a qualifying disclosure in the right way are protected from detriment and dismissal. Protection depends on factors such as a reasonable belief that the disclosure is in the public interest and that it tends to show one of the listed types of wrongdoing, and on whether the disclosure was made to an appropriate recipient. Disclosure first to an employer is the most secure route. Disclosure to a prescribed person, such as a regulator, is also protected under certain conditions. Wider disclosure has stricter conditions, and information protected by the Official Secrets Act raises additional issues. Anonymous concerns can be raised, but they are harder to investigate and may not allow the person to be protected. A manager should also know about malicious or knowingly false reports. These are not protected, but a concern made in good faith that turns out to be mistaken is protected. Managers should never discourage reporting by suggesting that raising concerns damages careers.

questions.prompt: A civil servant raised a concern internally and believes it was not dealt with properly. What does the Code say they may do next?

options.text: Take it to the Civil Service Commission, which is independent of departments
Go to a national newspaper at once, because the internal route has already been tried
Raise it again with the same manager until a different answer is given
Accept the outcome, since the Code allows a concern to be raised only once

questions.hint: The Commission is the independent route after internal attempts.

questions.prompt: Which of these could the Civil Service Commission consider?

options.text: A dispute about pay and grading that the department has declined to review
A complaint from a civil servant who was asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Code
An appeal against a minister's decision on a policy proposal
A challenge to a supplier's decision to withdraw from a contract

questions.hint: The Commission's role is linked to the Code.

questions.prompt: What does protection under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 depend on?

options.text: The disclosure being witnessed and signed by a manager of the department concerned
The disclosure being made outside working hours and without using official equipment
The disclosure being cleared in advance by the department's press office
A reasonable belief that the disclosure is in the public interest and shows listed wrongdoing, made to an appropriate recipient

questions.hint: Statutory conditions apply to protection.

questions.prompt: Which route to disclosure generally gives the strongest protection?

options.text: Passing the information to a national newspaper at the outset
Posting the concern publicly on social media so it cannot be ignored
Raising it first with the employer through internal procedures
Sending the concern to an organisation that competes with the department

questions.hint: Internal first is the most secure route.

questions.prompt: Why are anonymous concerns generally harder to deal with?

options.text: They are not permitted under the Code and are discarded unread by whoever receives them
They are harder to investigate and may leave the person without protection
They are always treated as malicious until shown to be otherwise
They must be passed to the police before anyone else sees them

questions.hint: Anonymity limits follow-up questions and protection.

questions.prompt: A concern raised in good faith turns out to be mistaken. What is the usual position?

options.text: The person remains protected, because the test is reasonable belief and not being proved right
The person loses protection, because the concern was wrong
The person must withdraw the concern in writing and apologise
The person is treated as having made a knowingly false report

questions.hint: Good faith protects.

questions.prompt: How is a report known to be false, and made to harm someone, usually treated?

options.text: It is protected if it was made internally rather than externally
It is protected if the person making it was under stress at the time
It is protected the first time it is made
It is not protected, and may itself lead to action

questions.hint: Malicious reports are not protected.

questions.prompt: Which statement from a manager would most discourage reporting?

options.text: That concerns are taken seriously and looked at promptly
That the person will be told what will happen next and kept informed as it proceeds
That people who raise concerns tend to find that their careers suffer
That retaliation against people who report will not be tolerated

questions.hint: Discouragement is harmful, even if subtle.

questions.prompt: Why do Official Secrets Act issues complicate disclosing a concern outside the department?

options.text: The Act bans all contact with the press for every civil servant
The Act protects any disclosure that its author believes to be in the public interest
Information covered by the Act may not be released outside proper channels without risking an offence
The Act applies only to people who have already left the Civil Service

questions.hint: Care is needed because of the Act.

questions.prompt: A manager's concern was dismissed by their own director without explanation. Which next step fits the Code?

options.text: Consider the Commission or another independent route, if they believe it has not been properly addressed
Accept the director's decision as final, because the director is more senior
Circulate the concern to the wider department to put pressure on the director
Wait until the director moves job before raising it again

questions.hint: An independent route exists when internal ones fail.

items.title: L13: New starters who struggle: induction meets probation
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Equality Act 2010; departmental probation policies, GOV.UK
items.body: Some new starters have a difficult first few months: they make security mistakes, struggle with the work, or seem not to fit in. A manager has to work out what is happening before deciding what to do. A useful sequence is to diagnose, support, set expectations and review. Diagnose by looking at the facts. Is this a skills gap, a lack of clarity about expectations, a health issue, a disability that requires adjustments, a personal difficulty, or a conduct matter? Ask the person for their view, because they often see problems you do not. Consider the induction: did they receive the security briefing, access to the right systems and the training they need? A security mistake in week two may reflect a gap in induction, not carelessness, though it must still be reported. Support by offering training, a buddy, clearer instructions and reasonable adjustments, and by seeking advice from HR or occupational health. Set expectations in writing: what must improve, by when, how it will be measured and what support is available. Review at agreed intervals, recording progress honestly. Treat the person consistently with others, and avoid assumptions based on age, sex, race, disability, pregnancy or other protected characteristics. If the issue is a security breach, report it through security channels even while handling probation separately; one does not replace the other. If a pattern of serious misconduct emerges, the disciplinary route may be appropriate. Remember that probationers have the same rights to dignity and fair treatment as others. A manager who handles these cases well protects the person's wellbeing, the team's performance and the department's legal position.

questions.prompt: A new starter makes a security mistake in week two. What should the manager consider alongside reporting it?

options.text: Whether to dismiss the person at once, because security errors are never accidental
Whether it needs reporting at all, given how early in the job it happened
Whether to hold back from reporting it until the end of the probation period has been reached
Whether the induction covered the relevant rules, since the mistake may reflect a gap

questions.hint: Induction gaps matter, but the report is still made.

questions.prompt: What is the sensible first step with a new starter who seems to be struggling?

options.text: Place them on a formal improvement plan straight away to set the standard
Diagnose the cause, including asking the person for their own view
Move them to less visible work without explaining the reason
Ask a colleague to keep a close watch and report back

questions.hint: Understand before acting.

questions.prompt: Which possible cause of struggling should a manager check for early?

options.text: A deliberate wish to annoy the manager
A plan to leave the team at the first opportunity
A disability that needs reasonable adjustments
A reluctance to attend the training that is offered

questions.hint: Adjustments may be needed from day one.

questions.prompt: Why set expectations in writing for a struggling starter?

options.text: So the person knows what must improve, by when, how it will be measured and what support exists
So the manager can avoid further conversations about performance
So HR can decide the outcome without involving the manager
So the details can be shared with the rest of the team for support

questions.hint: Written expectations support fairness.

questions.prompt: Which factor should play no part in the manager's judgement of a struggling starter?

options.text: The evidence of their work measured against the objectives
The support and training they have been given so far
How long the difficulty has lasted
The person's age, sex, race or disability

questions.hint: Protected characteristics must not influence the decision.

questions.prompt: A new starter commits a serious security breach during probation. What is the right approach?

options.text: Deal with it only through the probation process
Report it through security channels and handle probation as a separate matter
Overlook it if the person seems genuinely sorry
Hold it back until the end of probation and then raise it

questions.hint: One route does not replace the other.

questions.prompt: Why review progress at agreed intervals?

options.text: So progress can be recorded honestly and support adjusted if needed
So the manager can end probation early if the person is below standard
So other managers can compare the person with new starters elsewhere
So the person remains under constant pressure to perform

questions.hint: Regular review supports fairness.

questions.prompt: When might the disciplinary route be more appropriate than probation support?

options.text: Where the person is simply slow to pick up the work
Where a pattern of serious misconduct has emerged
Where the person has asked for reasonable adjustments
Where the person has joined the team only recently

questions.hint: Misconduct differs from capability.

questions.prompt: What do probationers have in common with other members of staff?

options.text: A right to automatic confirmation at the end of probation
Rights to dignity that begin only once confirmed in post
A right to choose their own manager for reviews
The same rights to dignity and fair treatment

questions.hint: Rights apply from the start.

questions.prompt: Why should the manager ask the struggling new starter for their own view of the problem?

options.text: It lets the manager pass responsibility for the problem to the person
It removes the need for the manager to reach any decision
They often see causes or obstacles that the manager has missed
It satisfies a procedural step without affecting anything else

questions.hint: The person's view helps diagnosis.

items.title: L13: Sequencing recruitment checks and judging hard cases
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; Civil Service Recruitment Principles, GOV.UK
items.body: Recruitment checks involve sequencing and judgement, not just box-ticking. Sequence matters because each step depends on the last and because mistakes cost time. A sensible sequence is: the advert states requirements, including any nationality limits and the clearance level if known; applicants are assessed on merit; the successful candidate receives a conditional offer; the department collects identity and right-to-work documents, employment history and declarations of unspent convictions; higher vetting, where required, starts at the earliest point permitted; and a start date is agreed only when it is realistic. A manager must not let a candidate start work with access ahead of checks, but may decide whether the work they begin matches what they are cleared for. Hard cases test judgement. A candidate declares a conviction not mentioned at interview; the question is relevance, honesty and the department's policy, not shock. A candidate has lived abroad for much of the last few years; for baseline checks the department will decide what evidence is reasonable, and for higher vetting residence may matter more, so seek advice. A candidate's referee is unresponsive; the department may accept alternatives, but the manager should not invent a reference. A candidate's name differs between documents because of marriage or deed poll; the department will usually ask for linking evidence. A candidate has a different right to work position, such as time-limited permission; the checks must be repeated before it expires. A candidate asks you to speed things up because they have given notice. Be honest about what is in your control, and avoid promises you cannot keep. The principle throughout is consistency, proportion and respect for the person, and keeping those who decide, usually HR and security, in charge of decisions about checks.

questions.prompt: Which element belongs earliest in a sensible sequence for recruitment checks?

options.text: A start date agreed before any checks have begun
A decision on the probation outcome made at offer stage
An induction meeting held before the offer is made
An advert stating the requirements, including any nationality limits and the clearance level if known

questions.hint: Requirements should be clear from the beginning.

questions.prompt: Why agree a start date only when it is realistic?

options.text: Checks and clearance take time, and an unrealistic date puts pressure on controls
The start date fixes the person's pay and conditions for the whole of the probation period
A contract is invalid if the start date is earlier than the checks
The department cannot move a start date once it has been written down

questions.hint: Realistic dates reduce pressure.

questions.prompt: A candidate declares a conviction that was not mentioned at interview. What is the right approach?

options.text: Treat the omission at interview as clear evidence of dishonesty
Reject the candidate at once, without any further discussion
Consider its relevance to the role, the candidate's honesty and the department's policy
Ignore it, because the interview is a separate process from the checks

questions.hint: Relevance and policy decide.

questions.prompt: A candidate has lived abroad for much of the last few years. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Treat the residence abroad as grounds for refusal
Seek advice, because evidence requirements differ between baseline checks and higher vetting
Ignore it, since only UK residence is ever relevant
Ask the candidate to stay abroad until the checks are finished

questions.hint: Residence may matter more for higher vetting.

questions.prompt: A previous employer does not respond to a reference request. What should the manager do?

options.text: Follow the department's process, which may allow alternatives, and never invent a reference
Write a short reference based on what the candidate said at interview
Withdraw the offer, since an unanswered request counts as a failed check
Ask the candidate to nominate a friend to give a character reference

questions.hint: Do not fabricate evidence.

questions.prompt: A candidate's name differs between two documents. What is a common and innocent reason?

options.text: A deliberate attempt to hide a previous identity
A clerical error by the department that can be ignored
A difference that never matters for baseline checks
Marriage or deed poll, in which case linking evidence is usually requested

questions.hint: Ask for linking evidence.

questions.prompt: A candidate has time-limited permission to work. What follows?

options.text: Nothing further is needed once the first check has been completed
The candidate is dismissed automatically when the permission ends, without further steps
The right to work check must be repeated before the permission expires
The candidate must arrange the follow-up check entirely alone

questions.hint: Right to work can expire.

questions.prompt: A candidate who has given notice asks the manager to speed up the checks. What is the best response?

options.text: Promise a quick result to reassure the candidate, who is anxious about the notice period
Be honest about what is in your control and avoid promises you cannot keep
Suggest the candidate resigns now and waits for the outcome
Ask the checking team to skip a step to save time

questions.hint: Honesty about limits.

questions.prompt: Who should decide difficult check outcomes?

options.text: Those responsible for them, usually HR and security, not the line manager alone
The line manager alone, as the person who knows the post
The interview panel, using the interview scores
The candidate, after being shown all the evidence

questions.hint: Decisions stay with the responsible teams.

questions.prompt: Which principles should run through the handling of difficult cases?

options.text: Speed, secrecy and cost saving, applied equally to all candidates for the same role
Seniority, loyalty and discretion
Consistency, proportion and respect for the person
Convenience, flexibility and trust in referees

questions.hint: Fairness principles.

items.title: L13: Leaving the Civil Service: continuing duties
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Business Appointment Rules; Official Secrets Act 1989, GOV.UK
items.body: People who manage staff also manage leavers, and leaving raises its own checks. When someone resigns or retires, the manager has several responsibilities. Access should be removed on the last day, or earlier in sensitive cases. Passes, devices, keys and documents should be returned. Work should be handed over in a way that preserves records, and personal files should be separated from official ones. The leaver should be reminded that their duty of confidentiality continues, including under the Official Secrets Act 1989. Some leavers have particular obligations about taking up outside employment. The Business Appointment Rules aim to protect against concerns that a civil servant's decisions or access to information may be influenced by the prospect of future employment, or that a former civil servant might use privileged information or contacts for another organisation's benefit. In general, the rules require some leavers to seek approval before taking certain jobs or roles after they leave, particularly at senior levels or where the new employer has links with their past work. The departments and the independent advisory body apply the rules, and details vary with grade and the nature of the role. If you are managing someone who may move to an organisation that deals with your department, make sure they know the rules and consider whether they should step back from related decisions during the notice period. A leaver must not take away official papers or copies of data. Exit conversations can reveal concerns, so listen and pass on serious matters. Leavers who were cleared may also have a final security briefing, and their clearance does not transfer into private life.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a leaver's system and building access?

options.text: It should be kept for a month to allow handover queries
It should be transferred to a colleague who is covering the work while the post is being filled
It should remain in place until the leaver returns their pass
It should be removed on their last day, or earlier in sensitive cases

questions.hint: Access removal is time-critical.

questions.prompt: Which of these must a leaver hand back before going?

options.text: Personal notebooks used only for their own reference
Passes, devices, keys and any official documents
Personal phones that were never used for work
Personal clothing left at the office

questions.hint: Official items must be returned.

questions.prompt: What do the Business Appointment Rules aim to address?

options.text: Concerns that future employment might influence decisions, or that privileged information or contacts might be misused
The rate of pay a former civil servant can accept in a new job
The pension arrangements for people leaving early
The notice periods set in civil service contracts

questions.hint: They protect against conflicts at the point of leaving.

questions.prompt: Which leavers are most likely to have to seek approval before taking a new role?

options.text: Every leaver, whatever their role or the nature of the new job
Senior staff, or those whose new employer has links with their past official work
Only people who are retiring at the normal pension age
Only people who are moving to work for a charity

questions.hint: Seniority and links matter.

questions.prompt: A member of staff plans to join an organisation that deals with your department. What should the manager consider?

options.text: Telling them that their future job is none of the department's concern
Extending their notice period without giving a reason
Making them aware of the rules and whether they should step back from related decisions during the notice period
Ignoring it until they have actually left

questions.hint: Manage the conflict during the notice period.

questions.prompt: Why must leavers not take away copies of departmental data?

options.text: The data will be out of date by the time the leaver starts a new job elsewhere in the sector
The data belongs to the leaver after a period of two years
The data is subject to a standard retention period for contractors
The data remains official information and the duty of confidentiality continues

questions.hint: Official information stays official.

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of a well-run exit conversation?

options.text: It allows the manager to persuade the person to stay on in the team after they have resigned
It provides a chance to ask the person for a favourable reference
It replaces the need for a handover of the work
It may reveal concerns that identify problems the department should address

questions.hint: Listening helps the department.

questions.prompt: A leaver has held a clearance. What should the manager remember?

options.text: Clearance remains valid for any private employer for an agreed period
Clearance can be reused at any other department without further checks
Clearance relates to the role and does not transfer into private life, and a final security briefing may be given
Clearance lapses at once, with no continuing obligations

questions.hint: Clearance relates to the role.

questions.prompt: What should a good handover preserve?

options.text: The leaver's personal contacts and address book
Official records, with personal files separated from official ones
The leaver's login credentials, so that a successor can carry on using them for the same work
The leaver's private notes in their own words

questions.hint: Records matter.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the duty of confidentiality on leaving is correct?

options.text: It continues after leaving, including under the Official Secrets Act 1989
It ends when the notice period ends
It ends if the leaver joins another government department
It lapses after one year

questions.hint: The duty continues.
